book.title: The World as We Know It: From Natural Philosophy to Modern Science

evidence: academic press signal: Princeton University Press / Princeton University Press

argument.statement: The book argues that what we take as “scientific” knowledge rests on a natural philosophy shaped by people, institutions, and cultural assumptions, so the world we know was not inevitable.

book.rationale: The book provides a historical narrative on the development of scientific thought and its impact on our understanding of the world, making History the dominant frame with a strong connection to Science.
book.summary: From the award-winning author of Revolutionizing the Sciences, a monumental historical account of how we came to see the world through the lens of science Science is the basis of our assumptions about ourselves and our world, from ideas about our evolutionary past to our conceptions of the vast expanses of space and the smallest particles of matter. In this panoramic book, acclaimed historian of science Peter Dear uncovers the roots of such beliefs, revealing how they constitute a natural philosophy that has been developed and refined over the course of centuries—and how the world as we have come to know it was by no means inevitable. In a sweeping, multifaceted narrative, Dear describes some of the most breathtaking accomplishments in the advance of human knowledge, such as Isaac Newton’s laws of motion and gravitation, Carl Linnaeus’s taxonomy, Antoine Lavoisier’s new chemistry, Charles Darwin’s theory of evolution, and Albert Einstein’s theories of relativity. Challenging the notion that science is only about “making discoveries,” he shows how our world has been formed by people, institutions, and cultural assumptions, giving rise to disciplines ranging from biology and astrophysics to electromagnetism and the social sciences.
